content.rendered:
Animals can’t vote, but their lives are shaped by decisions made in parliament every day. That’s why we exist: to bring animals into the conversation, and to show that what’s good for animals is usually good for people and the planet too. This is a plain-language summary of what we’re campaigning for. It’s more detail than our election manifesto, and much shorter than our full policy platform, which sets out the evidence, legislation and reasoning behind every commitment.

We know change takes time, and that farmers, workers and communities need real support to get there. Nothing here is about punishing anyone. It’s about building something better, together.

Ending the cruellest farming and fishing practices

New Zealand’s animal welfare rules are meant to protect animals, but in practice they’re often inadequate, poorly enforced, or simply ignored. We want to ban the most intensive and harmful practices first: intensive winter grazing, breeding fast-growing chickens, live exports, mutilations, and bottom trawling. Longer term, we support a full transition away from animal farming, done fairly and with proper support for the people who currently depend on it.

We’ll push for:

  • An urgent ban on the cruellest, most intensive farming and fishing methods
  • A funded transition scheme so farmers can move to plant-based or other work on their own terms
  • Tighter standards and stronger enforcement of the Animal Welfare Act

Recognising animals as sentient, not property

Animals in New Zealand are currently classed as property under the law, with no enforceable right to a decent life. We want animal sentience properly written into legislation, not just mentioned in passing, and the outdated property classification abolished.

We’ll push for:

  • Legal recognition of animals as sentient beings, with real protections attached
  • An end to codes of practice that let industries sidestep the Animal Welfare Act
  • A future legal framework that treats animals as individuals, not commodities

Making healthy, plant-based food the easy choice

Right now, animal-based foods dominate menus in schools, hospitals and other public places, even where health alone should point the other way. We want plant-based meals to be the default option everywhere they’re served publicly, clearer labelling so people know what’s really in their food, and GST removed from fruit, vegetables, legumes and nuts.

We’ll push for:

  • Plant-based defaults in public institutions, with other options still available
  • Fair, transparent food labelling, including clear health and environmental information
  • GST removed from core plant-based foods to make healthy eating more affordable

An independent Commissioner for Animals

Animal welfare policy is currently overseen by the same government agency responsible for growing farming exports. That’s a genuine conflict of interest. We want an independent Commissioner for Animals, similar to the Commissioner for Children, with real power to hold agencies to account and champion animal protection nationally.

We’ll push for:

  • An independent Commissioner with investigative and enforcement powers
  • Proper funding for animal welfare research and policy
  • Accountability for the agencies currently responsible for enforcement

Fixing our pound and shelter system

Thousands of healthy, adoptable dogs are euthanised in council pounds every year, often simply because of overcrowding, short reclaim windows, or fees families can’t afford. We want rehoming to be the default nationwide, not the exception, and euthanasia used only ever as a genuine last resort.

We’ll push for:

  • Transparent public reporting from every council on outcomes for impounded animals
  • Fairer, more flexible reclaim processes and fees
  • Funded foster networks and widespread access to desexing

Smarter, more compassionate conservation

We care deeply about protecting native wildlife, and we know introduced species do cause real harm. But we don’t believe mass killing is the answer, especially for cats, where there’s often no reliable way to tell a community cat from a wild-living one. Habitat loss is the biggest driver of native species decline, and that’s where solutions should start.

We’ll push for:

  • An end to lethal, poison-based control methods for cats
  • Investment in desexing, Trap-Neuter-Return, and habitat restoration
  • Conservation policy guided by evidence, not by fear or blame

Veterinary care people can actually afford

For many families, a sudden vet bill means an impossible choice. We want veterinary care treated as essential, not a luxury: GST removed from vet services, more publicly funded clinics in underserved regions, and funded desexing and wildlife care so access doesn’t depend on income or postcode.

We’ll push for:

  • GST removed from all veterinary services
  • A national network of publicly funded and mobile veterinary clinics
  • Guaranteed funding for injured wildlife and desexing programmes

Getting money out of politics

Industries that profit from animal exploitation have far more access to political decision-makers than ordinary people do. We want donation caps, real-time lobbying transparency, and cooling-off periods so industry leaders can’t move straight into government roles overseeing their own sector.

We’ll push for:

  • Lower donation limits and stronger disclosure rules
  • Public, real-time reporting of lobbying meetings with government
  • Cooling-off periods between industry leadership and ministerial roles

Making sure AI is used responsibly around animals

Artificial intelligence already manages hundreds of thousands of farmed animals in New Zealand, through automated monitoring, feeding and even virtual fencing, with no law written to account for it. We want animal welfare built into how these systems are designed and regulated, before harmful practices become locked in.

We’ll push for:

  • Animal welfare requirements written into AI governance and the Animal Welfare Act
  • A ban on AI systems that increase confinement or remove meaningful human oversight
  • Independent validation of any AI system marketed as improving welfare

Recognising companion animals as family

For many people, a companion animal is part of the family. We want statutory bereavement leave for the loss of a companion animal, and short paid leave when a new animal joins a household, so people aren’t forced to use sick leave to grieve or settle a new pet in.

We’ll push for:

  • Up to five days’ statutory bereavement leave for the loss of a companion animal
  • Up to three days’ leave when a new companion animal joins the family
  • Emergency leave provisions that cover urgent animal care alongside human care

This is a summary. Every commitment above is backed by detailed policy, evidence and legislative proposals in our full 2026 policy platform. If you’d like the short version of why we exist, start with our election manifesto.
This summary can be downloaded as a PDF.

Practices that harm animals also harm people – from environmental degradation and public health risks to the social costs of ethical desensitisation. The AJP believes that human wellbeing is significantly enhanced when we make compassionate choices. Our policies outline actionable legal and social reforms that safeguard human health, support rural workers, promote social justice, and build a harmonious coexistence with the natural world.

title.rendered: AJP Transition to a Plant-Based Economy Policies Overview

content.rendered:
True climate action requires transforming our agricultural system. The AJP’s vision for a plant-based economy provides a clear roadmap to move away from animal exploitation while ensuring a supportive, financially secure transition for farmers, workers, and rural communities. By incentivising crop farming, food-tech innovation, and ecological restoration, we can build an economy that respects sentient life and honors our guardianship/kaitiakitanga of the land.

Download the AJP Transition to a plant-based economy policies pack PDF below

title.rendered: AJP Environmental and Economic Policies Overview

content.rendered:
Climate change and habitat loss pose urgent threats to both people and non-human animals, driven by fossil fuels, ecosystem destruction, and intensive animal agriculture. The Animal Justice Party advocates for decisive, systemic change – putting the wellbeing of all sentient beings at the forefront of environmental policy and legal protection.

Note: Read our dedicated policy page detailing the AJP’s commitment to a just transition to a plant-based economy that respects sentient life, protects public health and supports farmers.

The Animal Justice Party Aotearoa envisions a future rooted in compassion, non-violence, and strict legal protection for non-human animals. Guided by the precautionary principle and a commitment to systemic reform, our policies outline actionable pathways to abolish exploitation, protect wild ecosystems, and transition toward a humane, sustainable society.

title.rendered: Mitigate natural threats to wild animals

content.rendered:
AJP recognises that wild animals often suffer from causes of natural origin. In many cases, intervention can be appropriate to protect wild animals from threats that they are not able to cope with. 

There are many examples today of people and conservation agencies intervening to protect particularly endangered or charismatic species. For example, stranded whales or dolphins are often kept wet and efforts are made to refloat them; lost penguins are transported back to Antarctica; underweight yellow-eyed penguin/hoihoi chicks have been hand-reared until they can survive at sea; and following cyclone Gabrielle, wildlife stranded in mud and floodwaters were rescued. However, non-threatened and less charismatic species often suffer from similar threats. AJP wishes to see these existing efforts increased and expanded to other species. Research is also needed to understand the welfare of wild animals and how their flourishing can be ensured and legally protected. 

Key Objectives: 

1. Promote wild animal welfare science to better understand the lives of wild animals and how their flourishing and protection can be promoted. 

2. Redefine the functions of the Ministry of the Environment to include the promotion of wild animal welfare. 

3. Encourage other government and community agencies and local councils to consider the impacts of their policies on wild animal welfare where appropriate. 

Interim Measures: 

4. Establish protocols in local councils and environmental bodies for interventions to protect wild animals in the event of natural disasters. 

5. Support volunteer groups that protect wild animals from natural threats. 

6. Increase interventions to protect endangered species from natural threats. 

7. Establishment of a national research institute for the study of wild animal welfare and the design and implementation of impact assessments and protection strategies.

Wild animals are frequently harmed due to the design of urban structures, roads, and the activities of people who are often unaware of their impacts. To address these issues, AJP wishes to see greater integration of wildlife considerations into urban planning, road design and signage by way of impact assessments. This would require greater collaboration between local councils, urban planners, conservation groups and communities to develop wildlife-friendly infrastructure. 

Key Objectives: 

1. Require animal welfare impact assessments to be carried out in the design of all roading and urban development projects. Enact stricter regulations mandating designs that better protect wild animals, especially where they are particularly vulnerable. 

2. Raise awareness of impacts on wild animals through education and public engagement, encouraging more compassionate wildlife-friendly behaviour and fostering community-led conservation efforts. 

3. Promote rewilding projects in urban areas, using native species where possible, and the connection of existing habitats through wildlife corridors. 

4. Fund scientific research to better understand the impacts of roads and urban structures on wild animals, and the development of solutions to mitigate these impacts.

AJP supports greater protection and restoration of natural habitats and ecosystems. We recognise that the destruction or degradation of habitats and ecosystems causes direct harm to wild animals, and that both humans and wild animals are sustained by natural habitats and ecosystems. 

63% of Aotearoa’s land area has now been converted for human use, with animal agriculture being a primary historical cause of habitat destruction. By 1930, 39% of New Zealand’s land area had been cleared and transformed to make way for pastoral farming. This transformation of land involved destroying forests, draining wetlands and disrupting waterways, causing significant harm to natural ecosystems and free living animals, whose habitats were obliterated or disrupted. As of 2021, this remains largely unaddressed, with 42% of land converted for farming and 8% converted for forestry. In order to reverse this process, AJP would enable greater protection of native ecosystems along with the restoration of ecosystems, especially in areas currently used for animal agriculture. Pastoral farming is a highly inefficient use of land for food production, using far more land compared to other crops, but producing a fraction of the calories. Moving towards a plant-based food system and away from animal agriculture would allow us to free up significant areas of land to re-wild. 

Key Objectives: 

1. Restrict further habitat destruction, of both terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems. 

2. Ban bottom trawling 

3. Restrict seabed mining 

4. Redirect funds away from animal agriculture, through taxes and regulations, and towards plant-based agriculture and habitat restoration projects and practices, as outlined in our ‘Introduce tighter standards and enforcement for agricultural pollution’ and ‘Provide financial incentives for good environmental practices’ sub-policies under Objective 2 in our ‘Just Transition to a Plant-Based Economy’ policy. This redirection of funds would enable:
a. Reserves: Stronger protection of, and creation of more, land and marine reserves (including more Highly Protected Marine Areas) 
b. Restoration: Roll out restoration projects to restore habitats, including mangroves, peat bogs, forests, marine habitats and other natural ecosystems. Subsidise farmers and landowners actively restoring the land and associated ecosystems. 
c. Subsidise green community projects 
d. Create wildlife corridors (link to Objective 3: Protect Wildlife From Anthropogenic Harms) 

5. Implement educational programmes in schools, universities, and communities to promote awareness of the importance of living within our ecological limits, for the purpose of avoiding, remedying and mitigating the destruction of natural environments in which animals live. See Compassionate Education policy.

title.rendered: Ending trapping and hunting for population control

content.rendered:
AJP opposes the trapping and hunting of wild animals as a part of so-called ‘pest control’ activities. For AJP’s policy on hunting for entertainment, see: Hunting and Fishing policies. 

A lack of enforcement for existing codes of conduct means that inhumane practices persist with minimal accountability. This regulatory gap allows for the continuation of trapping and hunting methods that cause unnecessary suffering to animals. 

Key Objectives: 

1. Amend the Animal Welfare Act to prohibit the unnecessary killing and suffering of all animals, requiring that population control be carried out with humane and non-lethal methods, and ensuring that greater accountability and stricter enforcement methods are upheld. 

Interim Objectives: 

While working toward long-term legislative change, AJP supports introducing more stringent regulations and safeguards to minimise harm to wild animals. These include: 

1. Mandatory live cameras on traps to ensure compliance with animal welfare regulations and to facilitate immediate response once an animal is captured. Current legal requirements for trap checks every 12 hours are inadequate, and real-time monitoring would enable faster intervention to reduce suffering. 

2. Strict codes of conduct for hunting and trapping, making ethical guidelines enforceable in legislation, rather than voluntary. AJP will advocate for uniform and legally binding standards across all hunting and trapping activities. (aligns to Hunting and Fishing policies) 

3. Age restrictions to prohibit individuals under 18 from participating in trapping, hunting or any wild animal control activities that involve direct harm to animals. 

4. Stronger regulation of live trapping, ensuring that any continued use of live traps adheres to high welfare standards, with a focus on transitioning toward non-lethal population management solutions.

title.rendered: Ending the use of lethal biological agents and poisons for population control

content.rendered:
AJP opposes the use of lethal biological and poisons to control introduced species, for example Rabbit Haemorrhagic Virus Disease (RHDV) and poisons like 1080 and Brodifacoum. Instead, AJP advocates for humane, non-lethal, and species-specific methods of population management. 

Poisons and biological agents used for population control frequently cause intense and prolonged suffering, with some poisons and diseases taking hours or days to kill, leading to unnecessary animal distress. Research has shown that some commonly used poisons, such as those with a welfare impact score over 5.51, result in slow, painful deaths and must be reconsidered as part of a humane transition in wildlife management. 

Key Objectives: 

1. Ban the use of all lethal biological agents, including Rabbit Haemorrhagic Virus Disease (RHDV). 

2. Cease the use of all poisons, including 1080 and Brodifacoum aerial drops. 

3. Fund research into ethical, non-lethal alternatives for managing introduced species, such as:
a. Immunocontraceptives for population control 
b. Fencing and habitat modification to prevent overpopulation 
c. Non-toxic deterrents and repellents 

4. Ensure conservation efforts align with compassionate principles and recognise the sentience and intrinsic value of all animals.

AJP recognises that animals from both native and introduced species are sentient, and have rights to life and welfare. AJP further recognises that humans are responsible for the introduction of non-endemic species to Aotearoa, and as such it is our responsibility to implement the most compassionate solutions where such species pose ecological threats. These should be framed and carried out in the spirit of Te Tiriti o Waitangi. 

AJP supports valuing individual animals because they are sentient, not because of their species status as native or non-native. We oppose the demonisation of introduced species, and promote an understanding of them as animals living here as the direct result of human actions. With this in mind, AJP will work to raise awareness of the cruelty of current methods of controlling introduced species. 

At the same time, AJP recognises the threat that particular introduced species, alongside habitat destruction and ecological damage caused by humans, pose to our native ecosystems. AJP therefore advocates for humane methods of population control, and the redirection of funds from current ‘pest control’ initiatives, such as Predator Free NZ, towards research and development of nonviolent forms of population control, such as contraceptives. 

Key Objectives: 

1. Call for government and government-funded entities to cease the use of unscientific, emotive and vilifying terms (e.g. ‘pests’) to describe animals and the requisite amendments made to the Animal Welfare Act. 

2. Establish higher welfare standards for population control methods. 

3. Fund research into nonviolent alternatives to current methods of population control. 

4. Create a special task force to plan the phasing out of violent population control methods and work alongside environmental protection agencies to implement humane management of all species, endemic and introduced. This group would be responsible for developing policies that prioritise humane alternatives while balancing ecological concerns. 

5. Implement educational programmes in schools, universities, and communities to promote compassionate management of introduced species.

title.rendered: Overview – Protection of indigenous and non-indigenous wild animals

content.rendered:
The Animal Justice Party (AJP) recognises all wild animals (indigenous and non-indigenous) as individuals with unique needs and value. We believe that within Aotearoa New Zealand both native and introduced animals have a right to live their lives unimpeded and unharmed by human activities.

AJP recognises there can be conflicts between endemic and introduced animals, while emphasising the need for solutions that prioritise compassion and protection. We reject divisive language, hunting and the glorification of trapping and killing animals for conservation purposes. Fundamentally, wild animals deserve the same rights to liberty, health, and freedom from harm as domesticated animals, and this should be reflected in law by specifically including them under the protection of the Animal Welfare Act, rather than considering them “pests” for eradication. 

Key Objectives: 

1. Use compassionate approaches to manage introduced species. Implement non-lethal, humane and species-specific methods to address challenges posed by introduced animals while recognising their right to live without unnecessary harm. 

2. Protect and restore natural habitats. Preserve and enhance the environments where wild animals thrive, using whole-ecosystem approaches that benefit both native and introduced species. 

3. Shield wild animals from human-caused harms. Mandate practices that minimise the negative impacts of human activities, development and pollution on wild animals and their habitats. 

To find out more download the full policy PDF.

title.rendered: The Future of Zoos and Aquariums

content.rendered:
The Animal Justice Party (AJP) advocates for a fundamental reorientation of zoos and aquariums away from entertainment-driven models toward facilities that exist to serve the interests of animals themselves. Facilities that currently exhibit animals for public display must transition toward roles centred on rescue, veterinary care, rehabilitation and, where necessary, the provision of lifelong sanctuary. 

Where animals cannot be returned to the wild, their environments must be designed to approximate natural conditions as closely as possible, prioritising autonomy, social needs and behavioural expression. Public access, if permitted, must be strictly managed to ensure that it does not compromise animal wellbeing. 

To find out more download the full policy PDF.

title.rendered: The environmental impacts of animal-based research

content.rendered:
The Animal Justice Party of Aotearoa New Zealand (AJP) aims to ban all harmful forms of animal experimentation. AJP commits to promoting the use of compassionate research.

Animal-based research isn’t just an ethical issue. It also has significant environmental impacts that demand attention. The environmental cost of maintaining these practices contradicts commitments to sustainability and climate action.

Key Objectives:

Interim measures, while we work towards the AJP Policy Ending Animal testing, include:

  1. AJP will encourage the minimisation of the environmental impacts of animal-based research by requiring all research facilities, laboratories, and institutions engaged in animal research and testing, including academic, governmental, and private-sector organisations, to implement sustainable practices, reduce waste, and ensure compliance with relevant environmental regulations.

  2. AJP will support the adoption of the following measures by all research facilities and institutions:
  • Reduce, Refine, Replace (3Rs): Prioritise alternatives in order to replace animal testing where possible, refine methods to minimise environmental impact and reduce the number of animals used. Strengthen the adherence to the 3Rs.
  • Waste Management: Reduce reuse and recycle materials wherever possible, properly dispose of hazardous and biological waste in compliance with regulations and implement sustainable alternatives for animal bedding and feed where feasible.
  • Energy and Resource Efficiency: Utilise energy-efficient equipment and lighting in animal research facilities and optimise water usage in cleaning, animal care and laboratory operations.
  • Sustainable Procurement: Source laboratory supplies, animal feed and equipment from environmentally responsible suppliers and prioritise biodegradable or recyclable materials in research processes.
  • Reduction of Greenhouse Gas Emissions: Reduce transportation-related emissions by consolidating supply shipments and using local vendors when possible, implementing practices that minimise the release of harmful substances into the air and water.

title.rendered: Pet Refuge Support for Domestic Violence Survivors

content.rendered:
The AJP is committed to eliminating barriers that prevent people from escaping domestic violence, recognising that the safety of beloved companion animals is often the deciding factor that keeps victims trapped in dangerous situations. We acknowledge that New Zealand has the highest rate of domestic violence among OECD countries, combined with one of the highest rates of pet ownership globally, yet we have only one pet refuge service operating in Auckland. We propose establishing a nationwide network of pet refuge facilities to ensure no family stays in danger because they cannot safely care for their animals.

Key Objectives: 

  1. Advocacy for stronger legal penalties for those who threaten or harm animals as tools of domestic control.
  2. Establish a nationwide network of pet refuge facilities ensuring every region has accessible, safe temporary housing for companion animals affected by domestic violence
  3. Provide comprehensive support services including veterinary care, behavioural rehabilitation, and trauma recovery for animals who have experienced abuse
  4. Create integrated referral systems connecting domestic violence services with pet refuge facilities to streamline support for families
  5. Fund ongoing operations to ensure pet refuge services remain free for families escaping violence, removing financial barriers to safety
  6. Establish a 24/7 emergency hotline for immediate pet refuge placement needs and rapid response protocols for situations where pets are in immediate danger
  7. Develop and implement a comprehensive animal trauma rehabilitation programme that includes specialized behavioral therapy for abused animals, staff training in trauma recognition, and integrated therapeutic interventions that support the healing of both human survivors and their companion animals.

The full policy can be found here.

title.rendered: End the Private Sale and Use of Fireworks

content.rendered:
Fireworks cause preventable environmental damage, wildlife harm and animal distress across Aotearoa. The science is clear, and the public demand for change is overwhelming. This policy addresses the urgent need to protect our marine ecosystems, wildlife and companion animals from the harmful effects of explosive celebrations. 
The private use of fireworks in residential areas and sensitive environments creates unnecessary suffering and environmental contamination that is entirely preventable. By ending private fireworks sales and use, we can eliminate the majority of fireworks-related harm while transitioning to sustainable and animal friendly celebration alternatives.

See our policy document PDF for the full policy.

title.rendered: Ban Recreational Fishing and Fishing Competitions

content.rendered:
The Animal Justice Party Aotearoa NZ (AJP) is opposed to recreational fishing and fishing competitions. We are committed to an immediate and complete ban on these activities.

Recreational fishing involves catching fish for “sport”. This practice causes significant distress and suffering to fish and other marine life. Fishing competitions exacerbate these issues by encouraging the mass capture and killing of fish for prizes and recognition.

Recreational fishing inflicts considerable suffering on fish, who can experience pain and distress from being hooked, handled, and often released back into the water injured. Non-target species, such as birds, turtles, and marine mammals, can also become unintended victims through bycatch, and entanglement in lost, abandoned or discarded equipment, leading to injuries or death.

Fishing competitions promote the capture of large numbers of fish in a short period, often resulting in unethical practices and significant harm to fish populations. Many fish caught in these events suffer prolonged pain and stress, and their survival rates upon release are low, contributing to ecological imbalance.

Recreational fishing and fishing competitions are ethically indefensible and cause significant suffering to marine life. AJP advocates for non-violent, community-friendly entertainment that aligns with society’s concerns and ethical and moral principles, and does not exploit and undermine animals’ well-being.

title.rendered: Towards a Cruelty Free and Sustainable Fashion Industry

content.rendered: The Animal Justice Party Aotearoa NZ envisions a future where fashion is free from animal exploitation and environmental harm. We recognise that the use of animal-derived materials such as leather, wool, fur, down and exotic skins perpetuates cruel and unsustainable practices. Animals exploited for fashion, like those farmed for food or fibre, are sentient beings with their own personhood and rights, and their lives must not be commodified for human use.

The Animal Justice Party Aotearoa NZ (AJP) is committed to protecting the rights and dignity of animals exploited in the agricultural system, including at the point of slaughter. We reject the idea that killing animals for products can ever be truly humane, as it inherently violates their right to life. While working towards the complete abolition of animal slaughter, we advocate for urgent reforms to eliminate the most egregious practices, improve transparency and enforcement in slaughter facilities, and reduce suffering where it still occurs.

AJP advocates for the elimination of all inhumane methods of slaughter, as existing practices often prioritise efficiency and profit over animal welfare. We believe that no animal should endure unnecessary pain, fear or distress at the end of their life.

title.rendered: Independent Animal Welfare Governance to Reduce Harm

content.rendered: The Animal Justice Party (AJP) envisions a New Zealand where compassion, sustainability and ethical practices guide our treatment of animals. While we advocate for a complete transition to a plant-based farming system, we recognise that meaningful societal changes require time and a ‘Just Transition’. In the interim, we are committed to reducing the most severe harm and mistreatment of animals by improving oversight of farming practices and strengthening legislation to provide stronger protections and ensure higher welfare standards for all animals in Aotearoa.

The Animal Justice Party (AJP) envisions a New Zealand where compassion, sustainability and ethical practices guide our treatment of animals. While we ultimately seek a complete transition away from animal agriculture towards plant-based and cellular systems, we recognise the urgent need to reduce the suffering of animals who are currently trapped in this system. One of the most severe and widespread breaches of the five freedoms1 occurs during transport, particularly when animals are moved between farms, saleyards and slaughterhouses.

AJP calls for a complete overhaul of animal transport regulations to recognise the specific needs of each species, regardless of their intended use. While animal farming continues, we demand far stricter controls on journey times, space allowances, rest periods and handling practices, as well as the retention and strengthening of the live export ban. Our long-term vision remains the complete replacement of animal farming with ethical, sustainable alternatives, but until that is achieved, animals must be afforded the highest possible level of protection.

The Animal Justice Party Aotearoa New Zealand (AJP) is committed to ending harmful animal handling practices and advancing a system of care that upholds the dignity,rights and welfare of all animals used in agriculture. While our ultimate goal is to abolish all animal farming, we call for urgent reforms to eliminate cruel procedures, ensure prompt access to veterinary care, and establish humane handling standards rooted in compassion and respect for sentient beings.

Industrial farming often prioritises profit over animal welfare, leading to practices that cause unnecessary pain, distress and harm. AJP advocates for the elimination of harmful handling practices, ensuring access to veterinary care and legislative reform that prevents cruelty.

title.rendered: Ensuring adequate nutrition and health standards

content.rendered: The Animal Justice Party Aotearoa NZ (AJP) is committed to transforming New Zealand’s approach to animal nutrition and health in farming systems. While our long-term goal is to end animal agriculture, immediate reform is needed to address the widespread welfare harms caused by inadequate feeding practices, compromised health management and overreliance on pharmaceuticals in industrial farming. AJP supports stronger regulation, enforcement and a shift in priorities from production efficiency to animal well-being.

title.rendered: Ensuring adequate living conditions and environmental standards

content.rendered: The Animal Justice Party Aotearoa NZ (AJP) is working towards a future without animal agriculture. In the meantime, we are committed to addressing the widespread neglect of shelter, housing and environmental conditions that cause immense suffering to farmed animals. Despite existing legal protections, animals across New Zealand are routinely exposed to harsh weather, overcrowding and barren environments that deny them the ability to express natural behaviours. AJP is calling for urgent reforms to ensure farmed animals are afforded basic protections, dignity and care.

The Animal Justice Party Aotearoa New Zealand (AJP) is committed to transforming animal breeding and reproduction practices to uphold the rights, personhood and welfare of animals. While our long-term vision is to end all forms of animal agriculture, we recognise the urgent need to reform current breeding practices, which often prioritise production and profit at the expense of animal health, dignity and wellbeing. This policy addresses the ethical, legal and welfare concerns associated with genetic manipulation, reproductive control and growth-promoting technologies used in modern farming.

The Animal Justice Party Aotearoa NZ (AJP) advocates for the complete abolition of animal farming. All animals used in farming, regardless of the intended product or purpose, have an equal right to live free from suffering, exploitation and neglect. AJP supports a transition to a system that respects animal rights, protects the environment and promotes public health through plant-based, cellular and sustainable agriculture.

AJP believes that animal welfare and protection is a social justice issue intrinsically linked to other areas where the vulnerable are exploited, for example, human rights, labour rights and environmental justice.

There are several Commissions and Commissioners in New Zealand dedicated to improving these societal issues, such as the Human Rights Commission, the Climate Change Commission and the Children’s Commissioner. They provide independent information and recommendations to the Government.

Currently the regulation of the welfare of animals is the responsibility of the Minister of Primary Industries and the Minister of Agriculture. New Zealand does not have a Commissioner for Animals who is independent to the Government and who can advocate independently on animal welfare and protection issues.

To create a comprehensive and effective Animal Protection Policy, a new legislative framework must be established. This framework should address animal welfare, conservation, ethical treatment, and the enforcement of laws to ensure that animals are protected from cruelty and exploitation. Below is a proposed structure for legislative foundations that could guide the formulation of such a policy:

1. Define animal sentience in legislation

2. Strengthen legal protections recognising animals as sentient beings

3. Propose a new legislative framework with positive welfare obligations

4. Constitutional rights for nature: advocate for legal personhood for ecosystems and species

5. Abolish the legal classification of animals as property and grant animals legal rights

This will be achieved through dialogue, research, analysis and solutions-based reform proposals to inform legislative and policy change and to enable greater political accountability and more inclusive and just governance.

Law and policy reforms will be secured to create an animal welfare governance system that is transparent, in line with contemporary science and public expectations, and focuses on the wellbeing and protection of animals. These reforms in New Zealand will have the potential to set a precedent for the creation of large-scale change globally.

The shift in the international animal welfare and protection policy environment highlights the growing recognition of animal welfare as a critical issue on the global stage.

It is no longer viewed as peripheral but has become integral to discussions in regional and international policy forums.

This change is underscored by the emergence of an expanding framework of science-based standards, conventions, treaties, regulations, directives, and agreements.

The Animal Justice Party Aotearoa NZ (AJP) believes that all animals in Aotearoa deserve adequate representation in Parliament, to ensure they are protected from exploitation and mistreatment.

To strengthen the voice of animals, we are advocating for the independent position of Commissioner for Animals to be established. Animal welfare is currently regulated by the Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI). This is the same Government department responsible for seizing export opportunities and overseeing agriculture productivity. Decisions on animal welfare policies are being driven by industry stakeholders who are invested in profiting from the use of animals.

title.rendered: Legislation and Regulation Reform for Animal Protection

content.rendered:
AJP supports legislation and regulation that prioritises the well-being, protection and rights of animals as sentient beings, ensuring they are not subjected to exploitation, harm or cruelty. It is imperative that animal welfare and protection legislation is adequately resourced and equipped with robust compliance monitoring, appropriate penalties and regulatory enforcement capabilities.

Animal welfare legislation should be drafted with the sole intention of recognising animal sentience and protecting animals, without influence from industries that profit from their exploitation. The principles enshrined in the Animal Welfare Act 1999 must be enforceable, without loopholes that allow industries to evade responsibility by self-regulation. Until adequate animal protection legislation is in place, AJP will also campaign to remove and prohibit exemptions and inconsistencies that allow animal cruelty to occur (for example, codes of practice for the “welfare” of farmed animals).

Policy category summary: The AJP is committed to improving the well-being of people by creating a better world for non-human animals. The current economic system perpetuates harm to non-human animals whilst contributing to the exploitation and detriment of human well-being within these industries. People employed in exploitative animal industries often endure hazardous working conditions, low wages and psychological distress due to the inherently violent nature of the work. Whilst equally people employed in organisations that care for and protect animals face burnout and compassion fatigue from constantly witnessing and responding to animal distress. The ongoing detrimental risks for humans include antibiotic resistance and the spread of zoonotic diseases.

We wish to address these interconnected issues to prioritise the advancement of both non-human animalwellbeing and human wellbeing. We also advocate for increased nutritional knowledge and affordable access to a healthy diet and exercise opportunities for everyone. We support a compassionate approach to all our interactions with each other, human or non-human animal.

Policy category summary: Te Tiriti o Waitangi holds profound significance for Aotearoa New Zealand, shaping the nation’s foundation and fostering principles of justice, inclusivity, and cooperation. The AJP embraces this treaty and acknowledges its importance in guiding a compassionate, just and equitable relationship with animals. The treaty’s commitment to non-violent conflict resolution aligns with the AJP’s advocacy for compassionate conservation, emphasising ecological sustainability and social responsibility.

A just transition to a plant-based Aotearoa New Zealand reflects the essence of Te Tiriti o Waitangi, promoting harmony and respect for all beings within the nation’s diverse tapestry. Test

Policy category summary: The AJP is committed to transitioning to a wholly plant-based economy. We recognise that in Aotearoa New Zealand our economic model is currently deeply reliant on the use of animals for food, products and exports. And that for many New Zealanders there is a strong historic and cultural connection to animal farming. But this is now destroying our wildlife, polluting our water and changing our climate, as well as inflicting unnecessary suffering on millions of sentient beings. This model is inherently risky as an on-going economic strategy, as new technologies, consumer preferences, societal concerns and changes in global trade threaten to reduce long-term demand for animal products alongside increasing regulatory burdens.

We appreciate this transition will take time, and that it must happen alongside financial and transitional support for farmers and the development of attractive and affordable alternatives for both farmers and consumers. There are, however, steps we can take now that will make a huge positive impact. These include banning factory farming, tougher laws, regulations and enforcement mechanisms, supporting farm livelihood transitions, supporting innovation in food tech, and promoting and incentivising more compassionate and healthy dietary choices.

Shifting to a plant-based economy is the single most impactful change to reduce animal suffering, whilst addressing many of our most urgent economic, social and environmental challenges.

Policy category summary: The AJP recognises the profound impact of our lifestyles, economic metrics of success, dietary choices, and leisure activities on the environment. The core issue that urgently needs to be addressed is the current unsustainable trajectory, particularly in terms of environmental degradation. The AJP advocates for a paradigm shift in economic models, enabling an inclusion of externalities of the natural world, and a move away from short-term gain to long-term ecological sustainability, prioritising wellbeing over relentless growth, and emphasising the importance of sustainable and future focused change to ensure a balance between human activities and planetary boundaries.


We promote the adoption of circular economy principles, community-led initiatives, and local resilience measures to minimise negative impact on the ecological footprint. We envision a society that measures success, not only by economic metrics, but also by the health of ecosystems, the wellbeing of communities, and the ethical and moral treatment of non-human animals, aligning with a holistic and sustainable approach to living and thriving.

Policy category summary: The AJP envisions a world where ecosystems thrive, and biodiversity flourishes, fostering harmonious coexistence between humans and other animals. We aspire to a future where habitats are safeguarded, species abound, and the delicate balance of our planet’s natural systems endures for generations. The undeniable detrimental impact of animal agriculture and the current management of biodiversity and habitats necessitates urgent action. We advocate for a paradigm shift in agriculture towards efficient and productive land use without farming animals. This not only reduces ecological footprints but also creates opportunities for rewilding farmland, allowing natural ecosystems to flourish, and carbon sequestration. We support compassionate conservation measures, habitat restoration, and the implementation of policies to mitigate the impact of pollutants and pesticides, including ongoing and emerging environmental challenges.

In honouring the Māori worldview, we embrace the concept of Kaitiakitanga, recognising our responsibility as guardians of the land. We look back to traditional practices that emphasise respect for nature and integrate these principles as we seek to preserve biodiversity and also respect the cultural connection between humans, non-human animals and the environment. In doing so, we aim to forge a sustainable path forward, where ecosystems are safeguarded, and the richness of biodiversity is cherished and protected.

Urgently addressing climate change

The AJP is the only political party in Aotearoa New Zealand with a serious commitment to tackling major sources of emissions in ways which are credible, compassionate and aligned with climate science.


Policy category summary: We support a rapid reduction in animal agriculture (which is responsible for around half of Aotearoa New Zealand’s emissions) by transitioning to a plant-based economy, supporting farmers to grow produce instead of farming animals and addressing the profoundly detrimental impact of climate change on animals. Additionally, animals are extremely vulnerable to the storms, flooding and fires we continue to see in Aotearoa New Zealand as a result of climate change.

We support policies that reduce emissions, avoid unnecessary animal suffering, improve human and non-human animal health, and restore and expand our waterways, forests and wildlife. We reject ineffective solutions that aim to perpetuate the status quo. We are committed to supporting animals of all kinds to adapt to the changes in climate that are already underway, and that which are predicted, in order to create a sustainable future.

title.rendered: Protecting the rights of farmed animals

content.rendered:
Policy category summary: The AJP believes that all forms of animal farming are ethically and morally unjustifiable and unnecessary. Nevertheless, we recognise that certain uses of animals inflict greater suffering than others, prompting our focus on addressing and alleviating these specific harms through our policies. The AJP actively focuses on safeguarding the rights of farmed animals, particularly during the ongoing societal transition towards a plant-based economy. While ideally aiming for a world without animal farming, we acknowledge the urgency of addressing the challenges currently faced by farmed animals and advocate for humane treatment, improved living conditions, and overall well-being.

The AJP recognises that the shift towards a plant-based economy is pivotal in reducing the need to farm animals, and will endeavour to guide this transition with compassion and practical solutions.In envisioning a society that places value on the lives of farmed animals, and seeks non-animal alternatives to food products, we advocate for policies and practices that protect the rights of these animals fostering compassion, responsible farming practices, and the overall improvement, and advancement, of conditions in the evolving landscape of sustainable agriculture.

title.rendered: Ending the Use of All Animals for ‘Entertainment’

content.rendered:
The exploitation of animals for entertainment stems from humanity’s long-standing belief in our dominion over other species. In these situations, profit often takes precedence over animal welfare. As a result, animals are routinely exposed to danger, forced to perform risky acts for human amusement and financial gain. This practice repeatedly jeopardises their safety, health, and lives, treating them as disposable commodities rather than sentient beings deserving of respect and protection.  

This policy is a wide and generic policy providing breadth to support standalone policies for specific cases of animal use in entertainment, for example our Ban Greyhound Racing policy. This generic policy includes animals in zoos and aquaria, keeping cetaceans in captivity, agricultural and pastoral show animals (for example for riding), or chickens hatched to provide entertainment for children, and ensuring that animals are not reintroduced to circuses and all other uses.

AJP advocates for an end to animal exploitation for artistic, fashion, cultural, sporting  or entertainment purposes, and will work toward ensuring no animal is forced into a working life for ‘entertainment’ and/or gambling purposes.

Key Objectives: 

Ban the use of animals for entertainment purposes. 

Interim measures, while we work towards the complete ban, include:

  1. Ban all forms of animal ‘entertainment’ that are funded through or support gambling.
  2. Call for complete transparency of organisations that currently profit from animals in entertainment.
  3. Ban the breeding of all animal species for ‘sporting’ performance.
  4. Ban the forcing of animals to perform at high and peak levels.
  5. Implement rigorous inspections of zoos, wildlife parks and aquaria to ensure their facilities and staffing numbers are optimum for the animals.
  6. Support those needing help transitioning to alternative careers.

title.rendered: Ban Recreational Hunting and Hunting Competitions

content.rendered:
Recreational hunting involves the pursuit and killing of animals for ‘sport’. This practice not only causes unnecessary suffering to animals but also fosters a culture of violence and desensitisation towards animal life. Significant suffering is inflicted upon animals: they may endure prolonged pain from injuries before dying, and non-target species often become unintended victims. 

Hunting competitions exacerbate ethical concerns by incentivising the rapid, large-scale killing of animals for prizes and recognition. This pressure often leads to inhumane practices and a disregard for animal welfare. Current practices in some New Zealand schools encourage children to participate in the mass killing of animals, often framed as a game or competition, in which violence is normalised and young minds become desensitised to the suffering of living creatures. Activities like ‘Toss the Poss’ not only disrespect animal life but also teach children to view certain species as disposable, rather than as sentient beings with lives of inherent worth. 

Hunting promotes and normalises violence against animals, dulling society’s sensitivity to animal suffering. Instead of fostering a connection with nature and teaching responsible environmental stewardship, hunting promotes a harmful and oversimplified approach to wildlife management. 

New Zealand allows the hunting of an arbitrary and wide range of animals including, to name a few, deer, pigs, free-roaming cats, rabbits and various  bird species. Seasonal restrictions may apply or licences may be required. 

Hunting practices cause significant suffering across various species. For example: many animals are not killed instantly, resulting in painful wounds and prolonged suffering; injured animals that escape often face a slow, agonising death and the use of certain hunting methods, such as traps or particular types of ammunition, can increase the likelihood of non-fatal injuries. In the case of duck hunting, a seasonal activity, an estimated one million birds are affected annually, highlighting the scale of the issue.  These problems are not limited to any single species but are inherent risks in many forms of hunting.

The practice of hunting also disrupts local ecosystems and harms other wildlife in several ways: It can lead to habitat destruction or modification as hunters create access points or use methods that impact the environment; Non-target species may be accidentally injured or killed and the presence of hunters and their equipment can cause stress and behavioral changes in animals, affecting their natural patterns. Importantly, these harmful practices are unnecessary for wildlife management. New technologies,such as wildlife contraception, more humane methods for managing wildlife populations that do not involve lethal means which tend to be more effective in maintaining long-term ecological balance. 

Recreational hunting and hunting competitions are ethically indefensible and cause significant animal suffering. AJP advocates for non-violent, community-friendly entertainment that aligns with society’s progressive concerns and higher ethical and moral principles, and does not exploit and undermine animals’ well-being.

Key Objectives: 

  1. Ban all forms of recreational hunting.
  2. Ban hunting competitions.

Interim measures, while we work towards the ban, include:

  1. Strengthen enforcement of existing animal welfare laws.
  2. Call for an immediate ban on duck shooting.
  3. Call for an immediate ban on the hunting of feral cats.
  4. Enforce regulations to prevent children from participating in hunting activities, including ‘school gala days’.

In New Zealand, approximately 30 rodeo events are held every summer, featuring activities such as bareback bronc riding, saddle bronc riding, bull riding, steer wrestling, barrel racing, team roping, and calf roping. These events involve significant risks to animal welfare, resulting in injuries and fatalities.


Rodeos inherently involve cruelty, and we believe that they cannot be made safe through regulation. These events promote and normalise violence against animals, dulling society’s sensitivity to animal suffering. This is particularly concerning for children who learn a skewed perception of “acceptable” animal treatment, shaping their long-term attitudes towards animal welfare.

AJP advocates for non-violent, community-friendly entertainment that aligns with society’s progressive concerns and higher ethical and moral principles, and does not exploit and undermine animals’ well-being.

Key Objectives: 

  1. Ban all forms of rodeo activities involving animals. 

Interim measures, while we work towards the ban, include:

  1. Change advertising practices to remove ‘family-friendly’ messaging.
  2. Implement a rapid phase-out of all rodeo events within a specified timeframe to eliminate this source of animal cruelty.
  3. Increase funding and support for cruelty-free community sporting events.

The Animal Justice Party Aotearoa NZ (AJP) is opposed to all forms of horse racing and is committed to eliminating the use of animals for human ‘sport’ and ‘entertainment’.

Horse racing for profit includes flat racing, jumps racing, and harness racing. Horse racing in New Zealand is less associated with a sense of glamour of the past and is increasingly controversial owing to the inherent cruelty and risks involved. Every year, despite efforts to improve safety and regulate the industry, hundreds of horses suffer pain, stress, injuries, and even death as a result of being raced.  

Contrary to popular belief, horses do not willingly participate in racing; many have to be coerced into the starting gates, highlighting the inherent lack of consent in the activity.

AJP advocates for non-violent, community-friendly entertainment that aligns with society’s progressive concerns and higher ethical and moral principles, and does not exploit and undermine animals’ well-being

Key Objectives: 

  1. Ban all forms of horse racing in Aotearoa NZ. 

Interim measures, while we work towards the ban, include:

  1. Ensure full transparency and accountability by having a public birth to death registry  for all horses born into the racing industry, whether these horses perform in official events or not. 
  2. Decrease the number of race meetings to alleviate the pressure on horses and reduce the frequency of injuries and fatalities associated with racing.
  3. Prohibit cruel practices and tools, such as the use of whips, tongue ties and spurs.
  4. Prohibit the racing of horses under three years of age.
  5. End the slaughter of ex-racehorses. 
  6. Provide ex-racehorses with proper care, rehabilitation and rehoming for fulfilling post-racing life.
  7. Reallocate government funding and subsidies to transition those employed by the industry into non-exploitative jobs and careers.

Greyhound racing involves greyhounds chasing a motorised lure at high speed around or along a specialised track while spectators place bets on particular dogs to win. The inherently risky nature of racing, coupled with the industry’s dependence on over-breeding, gambling revenue and the incentive to win prize money, has led to a situation where the welfare of racing greyhounds is compromised. Over 40 percent of racing greyhounds suffer injuries while racing; some serious, some lethal. This is the case wherever it occurs, and as a result, greyhound racing remains legal in only a handful of countries.

We do not believe that the greyhound racing industry can be safely regulated for the animals. We also acknowledge the negative impacts of gambling on human mental health, domestic relationships, and financial stability. Over the past decade, three reviews have shed light on concerning practices within the greyhound racing industry in New Zealand, following which the industry has lost its social licence. 

AJP advocates for non-violent, community-friendly entertainment that aligns with society’s progressive concerns and higher ethical and moral principles and does not exploit and undermine animals’ well-being. 

Key Objectives: 

  1. Ban all forms of greyhound racing in Aotearoa NZ. 

Interim measures, while we work towards the ban, include:

  1. Promote full transparency and accountability in relation to deaths and injuries of all greyhounds born into the racing industry, both on and off the track.
  2. Recommend immediate restrictions to curb the breeding of greyhounds.
  3. Call for a reduction on the number of greyhounds each racing kennel is permitted to own.
  4. Support the SPCA’s ‘Good Life’ Recommendation.
  5. Support the animal advocacy agencies (SPCA, SAFE, HUHA, Dogwatch) who are committed to finding loving homes for greyhounds when a ban is enacted.
  6. Reallocate government funding and subsidies to transition those employed by the industry into non-exploitative jobs and careers.

With many animal experiments being harmful or unreliable, we need further funding and research into more ethical scientific experimentation. The end goal is to replace all harmful animal experiments with alternative methods. As reported by the MPI during 2021.

Over 300,000 animals were used in experiments in the name of Research, Testing and Teaching. Many of these animals were killed both in these experiments and simply for no longer being useful to the industry. We know that animal experiments are unreliable in regards to biomedical research and yet, we continue to experiment with animals committing invasive procedures that too often do not yield anything valuable. It is completely unethical for research institutions to breed thousands of animals each year, to perform painful and distressing experiments, and then discard them.

The full policy for Ending Animal Experimentation can be found here.

AJP will campaign for an amendment to include animals that are exported by air; except for specific cases such as companion animals being relocated or relocation for conservation efforts. Not only are the transportation methods often dangerous, cramped and not up to the standards defined in The Animal Welfare Act 1999, we have no control over the management or care of animals once they reach their destination country. This allows for the treatment of animals we have raised and transported, to be substandard and not in accordance with our animal welfare laws and codes.

The full policy for Extending the Live Export Ban can be found here.

Organizations such as SAFE, RNZSPCA, HUHA and NZAVS support the call for a Commissioner for Animals. These organisations are on the front lines, witnessing the inadequacies and are often powerless to act. Aotearoa prides itself on having high welfare standards but while there are animals housed inappropriately and being denied basic freedoms, we cannot claim this as truth.

AJPANZ proposes that the Commissioner for Animals will have the authority to undertake comprehensive reviews of the current system and work to repeal and amend any Codes that contradict the Animal Welfare Act 1999. 

We propose that the Commissioner for Animals will have legal jurisdiction over animal well-being, enabling adequate monitoring of all sectors. We will allocate appropriate resources to organisations like MPI and RNZSPCA to ensure they have the capability to uphold the Animal Welfare Act 1999 and we will ensure these organisations enact effective administration of this Act. 

An independent Commissioner for Animals should be equipped to propose changes to legislation and enforcement where basic requirements are being ignored or compromised.

The full policy for Commissioner for Animals can be found here.
